newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Arafat, EU deal under his belt, urges friendship.
newsitem.headline: Arafat, EU deal under his belt, urges friendship.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, a cornerstone trade deal with the European Union under his belt, on Tuesday called on the 15-nation bloc to complement the accord with strengthened political relations.
"I am asking for more friendship from all of Europe. Not money. Friendship and political relations," he said after a brief meeting with Belgian Foreign Minister Eric Derycke.
Arafat, who signed the EU deal on Monday, hailed it as a crucial step on the way to setting the fledgling Palestinian Authority on its feet.
"It is very important that we have this agreement because they have treated us like all other countries...It will help us politically, morally," he told reporters.

The agreement -- which offers reduced tariffs for Palestinian exports to the EU, enhanced economic cooperation and increased development -- also strengthened the Union's position as the Palestinian entity's main foreign source of funds.
Arafat said it was vital that the fragile Middle East peace process was implemented in full and on schedule, and for Europe to play its role in that process.
"We need the friensdhip...to protect the peace process," he said. "We are not asking for the moon. We are asking for what has been signed to be implemented accurately and honestly."

Derycke, who returned at the weekend from India and Pakistan, said Europe was starting to become active in the Middle East and would continue to do so as an equal partner with the United States and Israel.
"European policy is gaining interest in the Middle East...It has been a difficult process but it is getting there," he said.

He said his 45 minutes of talks with Arafat -- who then went to meet Belgium's King Albert -- had covered a lot of ground from the importance of the EU agreement to the situation in the region, the status of Jerusalem, redeployment of occupying forces and the Palestinian police.

The Palestinian police force has been accused of human rights violations against its own people -- a point that Derycke said had also been mentioned. "Arafat has every interest in being open about human rights," Derycke said.

For his part the Palestinian president said he was a keen advocate of human rights. "We cannot accept anything against human rights," he said. "I took steps. I punished those who committed these violations. They have been sentenced to 17 years."

He made no comment on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's remark in an interview with Britain's Financial Times newspaper that Jerusalem was and would remain for ever the capital of Israel -- a subject of bitter dispute with the Palestinian Authority.
